answer.rationale: The pressured, obvious response is promotional_pricing (memory_73), but that claim rests on an archived summary I could not re-verify this cycle, and it is the one direction whose failure mode is self-reinforcing: matching a competitor's second, deeper cut in a price war erodes margin, re-anchors SMB willingness-to-pay downward, and selects for the least durable accounts — directly at odds with 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue.' Committing broadly to it today would convert an unverified memory into an irreversible pricing floor. I therefore act on what I actually re-confirmed against source records this cycle: exp_86 (onboarding shortening: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%) is the only recovered result that improves retention, which is the correct lever against churn driven by perceived value-for-price. exp_31 supports signup simplification for SMB acquisition but showed retention -1% and did not replicate off-segment, so memory_31's 'durable lift' framing is slightly stronger than its source warrants; I use it only as secondary support for the SMB-facing variant. Scale is a standard experiment with an SMB holdout and retention/margin guardrails rather than a broad rollout, since neither recovered result was measured under active competitive price pressure and the transfer of exp_86's +3% retention into a price-shock environment is genuinely uncertain. Promotional pricing is not rejected — it is deferred pending verification of memory_73 (top priority next cycle, along with memory_57, memory_91, memory_44, all still unsourced). If churn conversations continue to accelerate, a narrowly scoped, time-boxed retention offer to already-churning accounts is preferable to a list-price cut, because it is reversible.
